title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial injection budgeting, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived and referenced by path in the manuscript bundle.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises operational safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior work therefore proposes tool‑grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair pipelines as means to reduce hallucination‑driven or constraint‑violating proposals. To produce reproducible evidence about whether such tool augmentation causally reduces unsafe NetOps proposals, we preregistered a paired experiment comparing a baseline LLM pipeline to a guarded pipeline that validates LLM candidates with a deterministic sandboxed validator.

Research question and contribution. The preregistered research question (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) asks: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Our contributions are (1) a complete, deterministic, preregistered paired experiment with archived execution and analysis artifacts for N=200 tasks; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for the preregistered causal estimand (ceiling/testability failure caused by shared generation semantics combined with a zero baseline unsafe rate); and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for informative repeats (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection to calibrate baseline unsafe rate, and use of exploratory reserves to estimate verifier ROC). All cited artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*, model_configuration.json, execution_manifest.json) are archived in the run bundle and referenced below.
sections.related_work:
LLMs are already applied to NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, automated remediation) and surveys/prototypes document architectures that augment LLMs with deterministic tools and validators to improve correctness [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; OJCOMS 2026]. Generate–validate–repair or divide–verify–refine pipelines have reduced constraint violations in experimental settings, but effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, generation semantics, and prompt design [openalex:W4412888330; openalex:W7161354925]. Red‑teaming and guardrail literature emphasize trade‑offs between false refusals and unblocked unsafe proposals and recommend workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations with deterministic sandboxing and archived scoring traces [TechRxiv:177004277; TechRxiv:177006109].

Positioning. Unlike prior prototype reports and architectural proposals, this work is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: we publish a preregistered confirmatory run with deterministic artifacts and analyze how concrete execution semantics (shared vs independent generation) and budget accounting interact with statistical estimands and testability. The paper therefore complements prior demonstrations by showing a real preregistered run whose design choices—documented in the execution manifest and model configuration artifacts—rendered the confirmatory hypothesis untestable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline defined on binary SAFE indicators (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) produced by a deterministic validator. The confirmatory design was paired binary with N=200 unique tasks paired across two pipelines; primary inferential test: exact two‑sided McNemar as implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10000 resamples with seed = 1729 (these analysis parameters and outputs are in analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Task generation and sampling. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using the preregistered RNG schedule (seed sequence beginning with seed = 42; per‑task generator seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful single‑AS topologies and intent families restricted to admin/mtu/vlan changes to avoid vendor‑specific features; task manifests appear in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative task entries are included under manuscript manifest examples (execution/representative_tasks entries). The preregistration split tasks into 'benign' and 'adversarial' clusters; adversarial prompts were generated by templated obfuscation transforms intended to increase baseline unsafe rates. The preregistration explicitly allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two independent LLM calls per pair) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per pair whose output is scored in both arms). The executed configuration used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json.

Pipelines, validator, and repairs. Compared pipelines were (1) baseline: LLM‑only candidate (no deterministic validation enforced), and (2) guarded: same LLM candidate validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a deterministic sandbox and, if configured, optionally repaired once. For this confirmatory run the guarded arm performed deterministic validation but no automatic repair application occurred for confirmatory episodes (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs). The validator produced structured traces with validation_before and validation_after blocks, parsed command counts, violation lists, and a final valid flag; those scoring JSONs live under execution/scoring/*.json and were the basis for binary outcome coding.

Generation semantics, budgeting, and rationale. The preregistration permitted shared generation to reduce model call budget if budget constrained; the run executed shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve calls and to keep the experiment within the hosted budget. Execution artifacts record model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json) while the preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400; this precise accounting appears in execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json and is central to the testability diagnosis below. The preregistration's power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (≈10–15) and budgeted for N=200 paired trials under independent per‑arm generation; that assumption is recorded in the preregistration metadata.

Analysis rules and missingness. The primary confirmatory analysis executed paired_binary_analysis_v1 producing the contingency table (n11, n10, n01, n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and bootstrap CI; analysis artifacts are under analysis/*. The preregistered missingness rules allowed one automatic retry per failed model call and replacement for contaminated tasks; a stopping rule would abort if technical failures exceeded 10% of pairs. No technical failures or replacements occurred (missingness_summary.csv and deterministic_reconciliation.json show zero failures and complete_pair_count = 200). Sensitivity analyses (treating technical failures as safe or unsafe) were available but unnecessary here since there were no technical failures.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest records: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs × 2 scorings derived from one shared LLM candidate per pair), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json). The model configuration declares requested_model = "gpt-5-mini" and independent_condition_generation = false (execution/model_configuration.json). Provider call audit entries in deterministic_reconciliation.json show hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, consistent with a single shared generation per pair.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Analysis condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv) reports baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). These numeric outputs are reproduced verbatim from analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative scoring diagnostics. Example scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and task-000001-guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across arms and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true in both validation_before and validation_after blocks. No repair_provider_trace entries appear for confirmatory episodes, confirming the guarded pipeline did not alter candidate content in these cases. Execution/responses/* files contain the canonical per‑pair generated configurations; representative response files include execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, task-000002-shared-initial.txt, and task-000003-shared-initial.txt.

Exploratory reserves and unused diagnostics. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs; the exploratory reserve was not used for confirmatory inference. analysis/contamination_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv show no contamination flags and zero missing pairs. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact documents consistent episode accounting and that all deterministic consistency checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of a testability/ceiling failure. Three archived, exact facts together explain why the preregistered causal hypothesis was untestable in this run:

1) Executed shared generation semantics: independent_condition_generation = false produced a single LLM candidate per task that was scored in both arms (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json). The provider call audit confirms one hosted model call per pair.

2) Observed zero baseline unsafe rate: the model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced candidates that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labelled SAFE for all sampled tasks (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv). With identical shared candidates, the guarded arm could not produce discordant outcomes absent repairs.

3) Budgeting trade‑off: using shared generation reduced model calls to 200 instead of 400 (execution/execution_manifest.json). That conserved budget but removed the per‑arm stochasticity required for discordant pairs in a McNemar paired comparison when repairs were not applied.

When a shared candidate is SAFE under the validator, scoring the same candidate in the guarded arm cannot create discordance (no n10 or n01) unless an automatic repair alters the candidate; because no automatic repairs were applied for confirmatory episodes, the contingency collapsed to unanimous concordance (n11 = 200) and the McNemar test is uninformative (p = 1.0, CI degenerate at 0.0). This is a reproducible, artifact‑grounded ceiling/testability failure for paired contrasts that require per‑arm variability.

Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑supported). The recommendations below follow directly from the preregistration and execution artifacts and are implementable without inventing new tooling:

1) Use independent per‑arm generation for causal paired contrasts. For N=200 pairs this requires ≈200 additional model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200); make this explicit in the preregistration and budget accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json documents the executed calls). Independent draws allow true stochastic contrasts and create potential discordant pairs needed for McNemar inference.

2) Calibrate adversarial injection to achieve a nonzero baseline unsafe rate. The power plan assumed baseline unsafe ≈10–15%; preregister an adversarial injection fraction or stronger adversarial transforms so that, under the target model, the baseline arm yields a measurable unsafe rate consistent with the power calculation recorded in the preregistration.

3) Use the exploratory reserve before confirmatory testing to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs. Run the preregistered exploratory sample (up to 50 tasks) and archive ROC estimates before committing to confirmatory hypothesis tests; store ROC artifacts under analysis/ and record chosen decision thresholds.

4) Make model‑call accounting explicit in preregistration and reports. Publish both planned maximum_model_calls and executed model_calls_used (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json) so readers can reproduce budget trade‑offs.

5) Prioritize independent per‑arm generation over wide multi‑model panels when budget constrained: paired causal contrasts require per‑arm variability; if only limited calls are possible, allocate them to independent draws rather than increasing the number of evaluated models.

Operational implications. This run does not demonstrate that verifiers are unnecessary or universally effective. Instead, it provides a deterministic, reproducible example showing how particular execution semantics and budgeting choices can invalidate a preregistered paired estimand. The scientific value is methodological: publishable reproducible artifacts and concrete guidance for designing informative confirmatory repeats.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) we publish a complete, deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we provide concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, exploratory ROC estimation) to design informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (execution/*, analysis/*).

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
